source.title: Intrinsic Task Symmetry Drives Generalization in Algorithmic Tasks

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. There are minor PDF-to-text extraction artifacts, but they do not prevent reading the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests delayed algorithmic generalization and symmetry-based progress using its own tasks and symmetry metrics. It does not reproduce the original studies' method exactly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training dynamics, symmetry-violation measures, and time-to-generalization results. Several values are presented only in figures, and the text does not give exact numerical values for them. Results cited from prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper trains small models on modular arithmetic, graph-distance and comparison tasks. It tracks memorization followed by later perfect test accuracy (V1). It also tests whether a continuous symmetry-violation measure tracks and anticipates the generalization onset (V2). It uses a different method from the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that acquiring intrinsic task symmetries is the primary driver of generalization, through a memorization, symmetry acquisition, geometric organization sequence. They say weight decay is not necessary and only helps organize representations afterwards, and that symmetry-prompting objectives causally accelerate grokking.
record.recipe_differences: The paper tests a symmetry-based account using modular arithmetic, graph metric completion, and comparison tasks, with task-specific symmetry metrics and auxiliary losses. It does not state that it reproduces the original studies' full training recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports task-dependent differences in the timing and sharpness of phase transitions. GrokFast accelerates generalization in some settings and delays convergence in others. It also reports that symmetry-enforcing objectives accelerate generalization across tested ranges of embedding initialization and output scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: Auxiliary losses penalizing violations of task symmetries reduce the steps needed to reach 100% test accuracy across tasks, and beat geometry priors and GrokFast. In a no-weight-decay MLP they cut time-to-generalization by up to two orders of magnitude.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explicitly enforcing a task's intrinsic symmetries shortens the grokking delay.

record.problems: The paper does not give exact numerical values in the text for many plotted results. It does not report uncertainty estimates for the results described here. V1's training-set-size trend is not tested; the mechanistic circuit and memorizing-component details in V2 are not measured; and the claimed dataset-size predictions in V5 are not tested.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix A and Figures 10–23 give task-specific training-dynamics plots; Figures 41–54 give task-specific acceleration plots; Figure 9 compares geometry-promoting priors and GrokFast as well as symmetry prompting. These plotted, task-by-task curves were not entered as separate rows because their values are figure-only and the text states the aggregate findings recorded in R2–R3. The figure-specific method comparisons are also not recorded separately where the prose does not state their individual outcomes.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks; whether test accuracy starts at chance.
Identification of a generalizing circuit (e.g. Fourier algorithm) forming gradually; removal of memorizing components.
Non-algorithmic data. Appendix E varies initialization and output scale but reports only that the symmetry loss still accelerates training, not whether delays switch on or off.
All; no LLM or realistic data.
Circuit efficiency, critical dataset size and ungrokking. The no-weight-decay run does not control implicit low-norm biases.
All; no optimizer or floating-point controls.

missing.what: Ordering result: low-dimensional geometric organization of embeddings emerges after perfect test accuracy, not before it
Delayed generalization after memorization in graph metric completion and comparison tasks; the paper says timing and sharpness vary by domain

record.verdict_notes: Nearly all quantitative results are figure-only, with no uncertainty reported. R3 and the bold-line part of R4 measure the authors' own intervention and should not count as tests of a version. The no-weight-decay result is often read against V5. However, V5 explicitly allows other low-norm biases and AdamW implicit biases are not controlled, so no V5 verdict is given.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks, and does not state that test accuracy starts at chance.
The paper measures task-symmetry violations and their relation to generalization, but does not identify a generalizing circuit or measure removal of memorizing components.

It does not test non-algorithmic data or whether initialization scale or weight norm switches grokking-like delays on or off. It reports symmetry-prompting results across ranges of initialization and output scaling, but not that claim.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is tested.
The paper tests modular addition without explicit weight decay, but does not measure circuit efficiency, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below such a size.
The paper does not identify and compare algorithms learned across runs.
The paper does not control or compare adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point limits in the softmax.

rows.subject: single-layer decoder-only Transformer (modular addition)
rows.operation_detail: Train on modular addition and track training and test accuracy over time.
rows.measure: Training and test accuracy over training; delayed transition to perfect test accuracy
rows.value: The text says the model reaches perfect training accuracy before symmetry acquisition and that perfect test accuracy is reached during symmetry acquisition; exact values and timing are figure only.
rows.note: The paper describes memorization followed by symmetry acquisition, with perfect test accuracy reached later. It does not state that test accuracy is initially at chance.
rows.check: The text states that perfect training accuracy comes first and perfect test accuracy later, but timing is shown only in figures. Chance-level starting accuracy is not stated. The training-set-size trend is not tested.

rows.subject: models across the paper's algorithmic tasks
rows.operation_detail: Track task-specific symmetry-violation metrics alongside test accuracy across training checkpoints.

conditions.value: modular arithmetic, graph metric completion, and comparison

rows.measure: Symmetry violation and whether the run has reached perfect test accuracy
rows.value: The text reports a soft threshold: runs below a characteristic symmetry-violation level reliably reach perfect test accuracy, while runs remaining above it do not.
rows.note: The paper describes the relationship across tasks and seeds but supplies no numeric threshold in the text.
rows.check: The measure is output-level symmetry consistency, not a circuit. The authors call the threshold soft and not perfectly sharp, and give no numeric threshold. It bears only on V2's 'continuous progress measure anticipates the jump' part.

rows.subject: models across the paper's algorithmic tasks
rows.operation_detail: Add auxiliary symmetry-prompting losses that penalize violations of task symmetries.

conditions.value: modular arithmetic, graph metric completion, and comparison

rows.measure: Training steps until test accuracy reaches 100%
rows.baseline: Baseline training without the auxiliary symmetry-prompting loss
rows.value: The paper states that symmetry-prompting strategies consistently reduce the number of training steps required to reach perfect test accuracy across tasks; exact values are figure only.
rows.note: The text reports a cross-task result but does not provide exact per-task step counts in prose.
rows.check: This is the study's own acceleration method (auxiliary symmetry loss) compared with a baseline, GrokFast and geometry priors. It measures how the induced loss shifts timing, not whether the generalizing mechanism forms gradually. It belongs under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: two-layer MLP on modular addition
rows.size_stated: two-layer MLP; other dimensions not stated
rows.operation_detail: Train without weight decay, and compare with a run adding symmetry constraints.

conditions.value: symmetry constraints added in the bold-line run

rows.baseline: Without explicit regularization, represented by the dashed line; exact baseline timing is figure only
rows.value: The text states that the model converges to perfect test accuracy without weight decay, and that adding symmetry constraints reduces time-to-generalization by up to two orders of magnitude.
rows.note: The no-weight-decay result shows that explicit weight decay is not necessary for perfect test accuracy in this setting. The paper does not report circuit efficiency or the dataset-size predictions in V5.
rows.check: The row mixes two things. The no-weight-decay baseline reaches perfect test accuracy. V5 allows 'another bias toward low norm', and the paper itself invokes implicit regularization, so the result can neither confirm nor refute V5. The symmetry-constraint run is the study's own method, not a V5 or V2 result. No dataset-size or ungrokking measure is reported.

relationships.condition: 1-layer Transformer on modular addition, p=113, 30% training split, AdamW with weight decay 1
relationships.reason: The model reaches perfect training accuracy early, and perfect test accuracy arrives later during 'symmetry acquisition' (R1).
relationships.display_finding: Perfect training accuracy arrived early, while perfect test accuracy appeared later during symmetry acquisition.

source_check.reason: Figure 6 and Section 6.1 describe early perfect training accuracy followed by later perfect test accuracy; Appendix F confirms the configuration. The training-set-size dependence is untested.

relationships.condition: Output-level symmetry-violation measure across modular arithmetic, graph metric completion and comparison tasks, 20 seeds each
relationships.reason: Symmetry violation falls continuously, and checkpoints below a soft threshold reliably reach perfect test accuracy (R2). This bears on the progress-measure part only, not on circuits.
relationships.display_finding: Symmetry violation falls continuously, and checkpoints below a soft threshold reliably reach perfect test accuracy.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Output-level symmetry-violation measure across modular arithmetic, graph metric completion and comparison tasks, 20 seeds each
source_check.reason: R2 supports the progress-measure component: Section 6.2 and Appendix B report decreasing symmetry violations and a soft threshold separating generalized from non-generalized checkpoints across 20 seeds per task. Circuit formation and removal of memorizing components are untested.

relationships.condition: Embedding-geometry (low-rank, helical) structure in the same tasks
relationships.reason: Based on the text (no row): structured geometry appears only after generalization, during a later 'geometric organization' stage. So geometry-based measures follow the jump rather than anticipating it.
relationships.display_finding: Low-rank and helical embedding geometry appeared only after generalization, during a later geometric organization stage.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Embedding-geometry (low-rank, helical) structure in the same tasks
source_check.reason: Late visible embedding organization is reported, but V2 does not require embedding compression or helical geometry to precede generalization. These measurements do not establish that generalizing circuits fail to form gradually or that memorizing components are not removed later.

relation.reason: Reports its own training dynamics and interventions bearing on algorithmic grokking and continuous progress measures.

tranche.reason: Tests delayed generalization and a symmetry-based progress criterion using task-specific output metrics and controlled auxiliary-loss interventions.

source_check.notes: No numerical symmetry threshold is stated; Appendix B describes maximum instance-level violations and checkpoint generalization status. Section 6.1 notes that geometry can arise near completion of symmetry acquisition, although it usually becomes visually apparent later; late geometry alone does not contradict V2.
